title: After seven years, a spacecraft company is releasing its Otters into the wild
gist: Starfish Space, a ~120-person satellite-servicing startup that has raised ~$150 million, will fly its first full Otter spacecraft on a Falcon 9 Transporter mission next month for NASA's $15 million SSPICY debris-inspection mission, its first commercial debris inspection contract, with five more Otters in production for docking, deorbit and life-extension work.

insights.claim: Starfish Space's founders, ex-Blue Origin engineers Trevor Bennett and Austin Link, target two markets: extending the life of large geostationary satellites and managing growing low-Earth-orbit constellations including deorbiting threats.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Mega-constellation growth creates demand for in-orbit servicing and debris removal, an emerging space-economy niche.

insights.claim: Starfish Space has about 120 employees, has raised about $150 million, buys its spacecraft bus from Astro Digital, and focuses on rendezvous, docking and long-life maneuvering software.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Capital-light, software-centric model; a candidate for future funding rounds or acquisition in space servicing.

insights.claim: NASA is paying Starfish Space $15 million for SSPICY, the first NASA-funded commercial debris inspection mission, in which a ~350 kg Otter will approach multiple defunct US satellites within hundreds of meters.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: NASA becoming an anchor customer validates commercial debris inspection as a government-procured service.
insights.locator: This will largely be a demonstration

insights.claim: The first full Otter will launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 Transporter rideshare mission next month, and Starfish has five more Otters in production for docking, deorbit and life-extension missions.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Success would de-risk a production pipeline; watch the mission outcome as a catalyst for the servicing sector.

insights.claim: Starfish's 2023 Otter Pup 1 was ejected prematurely at 330 degrees per second by a failed transfer vehicle and later lost a thruster, while Otter Pup 2 (2025) has closed to within 1 km of a target with docking expected in coming months.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Mixed demo history shows execution risk in rendezvous and proximity operations.

insights.claim: Starfish used its software to fly Impulse Space's Mira spacecraft after its primary mission, demonstrating autonomous rendezvous with a single lightweight camera and closed-loop guidance, navigation and control.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Software licensing to other spacecraft operators is a potential additional revenue line.
insights.locator: Starfish also partnered with Impulse Space
